title: Researchers Demonstrate a New Way to Identify the Quantum W State
summary:
In quantum mechanics, particles such as photons can become "entangled." They are linked so deeply that their properties cannot be fully described independently, so the system must be treated as a whole. This clashes with the classical expectation that each particle has its own separate reality, a feature of quantum mechanics that famously troubled Albert Einstein. Yet entanglement is now considered essential for emerging quantum technologies, including advanced communication, computing, and information transfer.

There is a challenge, though. To build those technologies, scientists must create multi-photon entangled states and also work out efficiently which type of state they have produced. One standard approach, quantum tomography, reconstructs a quantum state by making many measurements. The amount of data it needs rises exponentially as more photons are added.

An entangled measurement offers a potentially much more efficient alternative. Instead of collecting many measurements and rebuilding the state afterward, it can identify an entangled state in one shot. Scientists had already done this for the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state, one of the best known forms of multi-photon entanglement. But no comparable method had been proposed or experimentally demonstrated for the W state, another important type of entangled multi-photon state.

Researchers at Kyoto University and Hiroshima University set out to address that missing capability. "More than 25 years after the initial proposal concerning the entangled measurement for GHZ states, we have finally obtained the entangled measurement for the W state as well, with genuine experimental demonstration for 3-photon W states," says corresponding author Shigeki Takeuchi.

The team built their approach around a mathematical property of the W state called cyclic shift symmetry. In simple terms, the arrangement of the photons can be shifted in a repeating cycle while preserving an important underlying pattern. Using this symmetry, they theoretically developed an entangled measurement based on a photonic quantum circuit that performs a quantum Fourier transformation. In principle, the method can be applied to W states with any number of photons.

The researchers then built a device and tested the idea with three photons. By sending in three individual photons with carefully selected polarization states, they showed that the system could distinguish among different types of three-photon W states. The team also measured the fidelity of the entangled measurement, which indicates how reliably the device produces the correct result.

The advance could have implications for quantum teleportation, which transfers quantum information, not matter, from one location to another using entanglement. The approach could also contribute to new quantum communication protocols, methods for transferring multi-photon entangled states, and new forms of measurement-based quantum computing. Takeuchi says, "In order to accelerate the research and development of quantum technologies, it is crucial to deepen our understanding of basic concepts to come up with innovative ideas."
why_it_matters: Quantum technologies need efficient ways to tell which entangled state has been made, and this approach could help with that. The authors say it could contribute to quantum communication and measurement-based quantum computing.
